title: Social Anxiety & Fear of Judgement
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

glossary.definition: An expectation about what others are thinking, often without direct evidence.
glossary.example: Someone assumes classmates are criticising them because two people looked up.
glossary.limit: A prediction can be tested; it is not itself an observation.

glossary.definition: Paying close attention to one's own appearance and behaviour during an interaction.
glossary.example: A student checks their hands and posture instead of hearing the discussion.
glossary.limit: Monitoring may feel protective while reducing attention to external information.

glossary.definition: Something done mainly to prevent a feared social outcome.
glossary.example: Someone silently rehearses every line so they cannot appear foolish.
glossary.limit: The action may lower anxiety while preventing them from learning what happens without it.

glossary.limit: A useful experiment checks the feared prediction rather than demanding that anxiety disappear.

nodes.title: Start here

nodes.title: What predicted judgement means
nodes.body:
An expectation about what others are thinking, often without direct evidence.

For example: Someone assumes classmates are criticising them because two people looked up.

One important limit: A prediction can be tested; it is not itself an observation.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Owen is arriving at a seminar with unfamiliar classmates. Leah walks in with him.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.
nodes.scenario: Owen is arriving at a seminar with unfamiliar classmates. Leah walks in with him.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: I think everyone noticed how awkward I looked coming in.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What did you see them do?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Two people looked up when I opened the door.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Did either of them actually react to you?

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.
checks.counterexample: Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.

items.label: “I think everyone noticed how awkward I looked coming in.”
Owen relies heavily on an internal impression of how he appears. Self-focused attention leaves him with less external evidence, which can make his feared judgement seem more convincing.
“What did you see them do?”
The group could be dismissive or unwelcoming; social fears sometimes reflect actual interpersonal experiences.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Owen relies heavily on an internal impression of how he appears. Self-focused attention leaves him with less external evidence, which can make his feared judgement seem more convincing.

Another possibility: The group could be dismissive or unwelcoming; social fears sometimes reflect actual interpersonal experiences.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Compare his predicted reactions with observable behaviour rather than using the intensity of anxiety as the sole evidence. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Compare his predicted reactions with observable behaviour rather than using the intensity of anxiety as the sole evidence.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: A classmate later invites Owen to join their discussion and refers positively to a question he asked.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The new social response weakens Owen's broad conclusion that everyone judged him badly, without proving that every classmate felt positively.
nodes.counterexample: Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), cognitive model of social phobia.
nodes.scenario: Milo enters a society meeting where he knows nobody.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Everyone can tell I don't belong here.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: What did you see people do?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Two glanced at the door. Now I'm checking how I'm standing.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Does focusing on your posture help you join in?

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Not really. I keep rehearsing a sentence and missing what people say.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: Could you listen for one thing to ask them about?

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: The group may genuinely have treated newcomers as unwelcome.

Owen relies heavily on an internal impression of how he appears. Self-focused attention leaves him with less external evidence, which can make his feared judgement seem more convincing.
The meaning of the event may differ between the speakers, even when they agree about the observable facts.
evidenceOptions.feedback: Different interpretations may contribute, but this is not yet specific enough to explain the response.

evidenceOptions.label: The immediate context may account for more of the reaction than a stable personal tendency would.
evidenceOptions.feedback: Situation-specific pressure is plausible, though the evidence may indicate an additional process.

responseOptions.label: Stop attending seminars until you can enter without feeling nervous.
Try giving the conversation your attention and afterwards compare your prediction with what people actually said or did.

responseOptions.feedback: This may be helpful at another stage. We still need a response that fits the practical aim and the current evidence.

responseOptions.label: Seek agreement on a specific next step, then check whether it actually addresses the concern.
responseOptions.feedback: A jointly agreed next step is reasonable, though the other person may still decline.

nodes.title: What might change next?
nodes.prompt: The other person may disagree. Which response-and-outcome pairing best protects the practical concern without assuming cooperation?
nodes.conceptId: social-anxiety-module-01:Self-focused attention, safety behaviours and post-event appraisal
nodes.explanation: A sound response is judged by what it makes possible, not by whether it can instantly change somebody else. Try giving the conversation your attention and afterwards compare your prediction with what people actually said or did.
nodes.counterexample: Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.

outcomes.label: The other person’s interpretation may become clearer, though the original issue may still need to be resolved.

The immediate tension may ease without settling the underlying concern or establishing anyone’s motive.
outcomes.feedback: Short-term relief is possible, but the question asks what the proposed response would most directly change.

nodes.title: If the first response fails
nodes.prompt: The other person rejects a reasonable direct request and the practical concern is unresolved. What next?
nodes.conceptId: social-anxiety-module-01:Self-focused attention, safety behaviours and post-event appraisal
nodes.explanation: Escalation can be proportionate when a direct attempt has failed. Its safety and usefulness depend on the situation. Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.

options.label: Repeat reassurance until the other person no longer experiences the issue as threatening.
options.feedback: Reassurance can help but cannot guarantee action on a concrete problem.

options.label: Stop attending seminars until you can enter without feeling nervous.
options.feedback: This makes the unresolved issue reviewable without needing to diagnose the other person.

options.label: A previous disagreement may have shaped the response, making the present conversation part of a longer pattern.
options.feedback: History could matter, but that earlier pattern has not yet been established.

options.label: What did people do that supports the judgement, apart from looking in your direction?
options.feedback: A further question can clarify motives, but may delay resolution when the refusal is already clear.

options.label: Owen may be noticing real social cues while giving them greater negative weight than the evidence supports.
options.feedback: The classmates did look up; the leap is from noticing to hostile judgement.

nodes.title: Correct the inference
nodes.prompt: Someone says: “That tells us what sort of person they really are.” Which revision is most defensible?

nodes.explanation: A working interpretation can be informative without being a diagnosis. Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.

options.label: Because an alternative is possible, every explanation should be treated as equally likely until we know the person well.
options.feedback: Possible explanations need not be equally supported. We should compare their fit with the actual evidence.

options.label: The behaviour may serve the proposed function in this case. We would need broader evidence before treating it as a stable characteristic.
options.feedback: This retains a useful process explanation without generalising beyond the evidence.

options.feedback: Direct self-report helps, but a tentative formulation can still be tested against observed circumstances.

nodes.title: Which evidence matters most?
nodes.prompt: You want to distinguish the working hypothesis from its strongest alternative. Which investigation would provide the most discriminating information?
nodes.conceptId: social-anxiety-module-01:Self-focused attention, safety behaviours and post-event appraisal
nodes.explanation: Investigate a difference that the rival explanations predict. Compare his predicted reactions with observable behaviour rather than using the intensity of anxiety as the sole evidence.
nodes.counterexample: Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.

options.label: Ask both people to describe how strongly they felt during the conversation.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling matters, but it does not establish its cause.

options.label: Compare his predicted reactions with observable behaviour rather than using the intensity of anxiety as the sole evidence.
options.feedback: This gathers information that could strengthen or weaken the explanation, rather than merely confirming an impression.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.
options.feedback: Impact and perception matter for responding; they are less decisive about the other person’s hidden motives.

options.label: Find one more occasion when the characters disagreed, without checking what the circumstances were.
options.feedback: Another incident is useful only if we compare the circumstances and plausible explanations.

options.label: Examine whether a similar response occurs when the immediate practical stakes are different.
options.feedback: A pattern could test generalisation, although the settings may not be comparable.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
During a group conversation, somebody watches their facial expression closely and later judges the whole encounter from how awkward they felt rather than what others actually did.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

steps.label: Owen enters a socially evaluative situation
He predicts other people are judging his appearance
He monitors his own movements and rehearses responses
Reduced attention to others leaves the prediction largely untested

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Owen relies heavily on an internal impression of how he appears. Self-focused attention leaves him with less external evidence, which can make his feared judgement seem more convincing.

Looking up when somebody enters is not equivalent to hostile scrutiny. At the same time, an anxious interpretation cannot be disproved solely by telling someone not to worry.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.
nodes.sources: Clark & Wells (1995), social phobia model; NICE CG159 social anxiety disorder guidance.

glossary.definition: An expectation about what others are thinking, often without direct evidence.
glossary.example: Someone assumes classmates are criticising them because two people looked up.
glossary.limit: A prediction can be tested; it is not itself an observation.

glossary.definition: Paying close attention to one's own appearance and behaviour during an interaction.
glossary.example: A student checks their hands and posture instead of hearing the discussion.
glossary.limit: Monitoring may feel protective while reducing attention to external information.

glossary.definition: Something done mainly to prevent a feared social outcome.
glossary.example: Someone silently rehearses every line so they cannot appear foolish.
glossary.limit: The action may lower anxiety while preventing them from learning what happens without it.

glossary.definition: A planned way of comparing a prediction with an observable result.
glossary.example: A student listens to the conversation, asks one question and records the actual response.
glossary.limit: A useful experiment checks the feared prediction rather than demanding that anxiety disappear.
